altText: A bronze sculpture of the Buddha standing upright, about half a meter tall. Silver is set into the dark metal surface.

context: A bronze statue of the Buddha standing, made in Burma during the Pagan period, in the 12th or 13th century. Silver is inlaid into the bronze, and the figure is about 50.5 cm tall. The catalog page gives no label text, so its details beyond the title and materials are not described in the record.

descriptions.k: This is a bronze statue of the Buddha. He is standing tall. It was made in Burma long ago. Silver is set into the dark metal. It adds a shine. Can you find the silver?
descriptions.g12: A maker in Burma, which is also called Myanmar, cast this Buddha in bronze about 800 years ago. He stands tall and still. Silver is set into the dark metal to add sparkle. The statue is about half a meter tall, longer than a ruler. What does his standing pose tell you about him?
descriptions.g35: This standing Buddha was made in Burma during the Pagan period, about 800 to 900 years ago. It is cast in bronze, and silver was set into the surface, a technique called inlay. The statue is about 50 centimeters tall. Look at how the figure stands and where the silver shines. How do the metals make the statue special?
descriptions.g68: Made in Burma in the Pagan period, in the 12th or 13th century, this standing Buddha is bronze with silver inlay. Inlay means setting one material into another, so the silver adds contrast and shine to the dark bronze. At about 50.5 cm tall, it may have been meant for a shrine or small temple, though the record does not say. How do posture, material, and inlay combine to show reverence for the Buddha?
descriptions.g910: This bronze Buddha, standing about 50.5 cm tall, comes from Pagan-period Burma, the 12th or 13th century, and is enriched with silver inlay. Inlay adds a contrast of metal and tone that draws attention to selected areas, though the record does not specify which. The upright pose offers a frontal, stable presence suited to devotion. How do metals, posture, and scale shape the object's presence, and how does the museum record limit what we can say?
descriptions.g1112: Pagan-period metalwork is often admired for its refinement, and this standing Buddha in bronze with silver inlay illustrates the care lavished on devotional images. The combination of metals introduces contrast of color and reflectivity, a deliberate enhancement of surface. Because the record offers little label text, interpretation should remain cautious about its original setting, patronage, and ritual function. Consider how material richness, frontal pose, and modest scale produced a sense of presence, and how the museum changes that experience.

k.space: The statue is about as tall as one and a half rulers. How big would it look next to you?
k.light: Where does the light make the silver sparkle?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, classification (Sculpture), medium (Bronze with silver inlay), culture, and tags (Buddhism, Buddha) checked against the museum record. The catalog page has no label text, so descriptions rely on the title, materials, size, and general Buddhist iconography. Bare-chested depiction could not be ruled out from metadata alone, so descriptions avoid body detail.

teacherNote.context: A standing Buddha in bronze with silver inlay from Pagan-period Burma (12th-13th century), about 50.5 cm tall. The record offers no label text on pose or use.
directions: Ask students to compare this figure with a seated or walking Buddha elsewhere in the archive and note what changes with the pose.
Discuss how two materials can be combined for contrast, using examples from students' lives.
Practice respectful language for discussing sacred objects from other traditions.
